Peamouth (Mylocheilus caurinus) is a cyprinid fish endemic to the Pacific Northwest, where it inhabits lakes and slow-moving rivers from the Columbia River basin northward. Field surveys conducted across several British Columbia populations indicate that sexually mature individuals typically first attain puberty at a total length of approximately 21 cm [Lp = approximately 21 cm]. This length threshold corresponds to a wet weight at puberty estimated at roughly 180 grams [Wwp = roughly 180 grams], a body size that appears to be a reliable predictor of the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both males and females. The timing of this developmental milestone is closely tied to local thermal regimes, as water temperature strongly influences growth rates in juvenile peamouth. Comparisons with other cyprinids of similar body plan suggest that the length at puberty recorded for M. caurinus falls within the expected range for a moderately sized, iteroparous freshwater species. Despite its relatively modest body size, this species exhibits a life history strategy characterized by delayed maturation relative to some smaller lacustrine cyprinids, which may reflect the energetic demands of seasonal spawning migrations into tributary streams.

Spawning events in peamouth typically occur during the late spring and early summer when water temperatures rise, prompting reproductive adults to aggregate in gravel-bottomed riffles of tributary creeks. Gravid females produce adhesive, demersal eggs that are broadcast over the substrate during gametic union; no parental care is provided following the spawning event. The incubation period of the fertilized ova is temperature-dependent, and in laboratory rearing trials conducted at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after approximately two weeks. Under these controlled thermal conditions, the total lifespan of the species has been estimated at roughly 5.5 years [am = roughly 5.5 years], a maximum longevity derived from mark-recapture studies of wild individuals at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a cyprinid of its size and aligns with the pace of life expected for a fish that allocates considerable somatic growth to reaching a substantial adult body size before senescent mortality becomes prevalent. Factors such as predation pressure and food availability in lentic habitats likely modulate whether individuals approach this upper bound.

The neonatal wet weight at birth for M. caurinus is remarkably low, reflecting the small size of its yolky, demersal eggs. Based on an average egg diameter of approximately 1.165 mm, the calculated wet weight of a newly hatched alevin is about 0.0024 grams [Wwb = about 0.0024 grams], placing the individual in a highly vulnerable, endotrophic larval stage. The prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-eclosion, a period of rapid morphological differentiation. Once the gape of the mouth opens and retinal differentiation permits prey detection, the free-swimming larva initiates first exogenous feeding, a critical trophic switch that determines subsequent survival. The transition from a lecithotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition is a period of high mortality in wild populations, as the tiny size of the predatory larvae limits the range of zooplanktonic prey they can effectively capture. This early life history stage thus represents a major demographic bottleneck, one that likely shapes year-class strength in fluctuating environmental conditions.

As peamouth individuals continue to grow beyond the postflexion larval stage, they begin a period of rapid somatic mass gain that carries them through the juvenile and sub-adult phases. At the upper end of the size spectrum, the largest recorded adults achieve an ultimate total length of 36 cm [Li = 36 cm], a size attained only by the oldest and fastest-growing individuals in the population. The asymptotic wet weight associated with this ultimate length is approximately 604 grams [Wwi = approximately 604 grams], a value that exceeds that of most other cyprinids of comparable standard length in the Pacific Northwest, reflecting the species' relatively robust body shape and its reliance on benthic invertebrate prey. This adult body mass is attained gradually over several growing seasons, with the most substantial increments occurring during the first three years of life when feeding intensity is highest. The relationship between length and weight in peamouth is well described by a power function typical of fusiform cyprinids, and the observed maximum mass is consistent with the species' position as a mid-sized omnivore within its lentic and lotic habitats. Seasonal fluctuations in condition factor are evident, with fish typically being heaviest in late autumn following the summer feeding period.

Water temperature constitutes a dominant abiotic factor governing the developmental rate and metabolic scope of M. caurinus throughout its life cycle. In contrast to the 16 °C [T = 16 °C] conditions under which lifespan was estimated, growth experiments have demonstrated that the species shows optimal feeding and swimming performance at temperatures slightly above this value. The relatively cool thermal optimum reflects the peamouth's evolutionary history in the temperate rivers and lakes of the Pacific drainage. The species has been observed to cease feeding at water temperatures below 4 °C [T = 4 °C] during winter months, entering a period of reduced metabolic activity. Field recapture data confirm that the maximum longevity of 5.5 years [am = 5.5 years] is attainable by both sexes, a lifespan comparable to other temperate cyprinids such as Ptychocheilus oregonensis, though considerably shorter than that of its larger-bodied relative Mylocheilus lateralis at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The interplay between thermal regime and resource availability thus defines the realized life history trajectory of this species.
